title: Al-Muqsit, the Equitable
tomorrow: Saturday, one wall, a lot of paint. who shows up?

lines: ONE DID HALF. ONE DID NONE.
FULL PRICE, OR A FREE PASS?
cards: A group project. One person made half the slides, one made none, and the grade is shared.
Fair can mean everyone gets the same, or it can mean everyone gets what they put in, and that argument shows up everywhere from group chats to courtrooms.
Yesterday's question: what's fair when the one who wronged you is thirteen? Full price? A free pass?
Today's Name lives in the space between.

teach.b: Al-Muqsit, the Equitable: the One who gives each their due, no thumb on the scale. The Qur'an tells believers, in Pickthall's words: "let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly."
And elsewhere: "Lo! Allah loveth the equitable." Notice what the first verse names as the danger. Not ignorance.
Anger. The moment you most want the scale to tip is the moment it has to stay level. Now a neighbor.

teach.h: LEVITICUS: NOT THE POOR, NOT THE MIGHTY.
teach.b: Jews and Christians read a line in Leviticus, in the King James words: "thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour."
That's the shared thing, and it's close: justice that refuses to lean. And here's the surprising part to tell a friend tonight.
Leviticus doesn't only warn against favoring the powerful. It warns against favoring the poor, too. Even sympathy isn't allowed to tilt the verdict.
The honest difference: Leviticus names status as the pull, poor or mighty, while the Qur'an's verse names hatred of a people. Each tradition is watching a different hand reach for the scale.
So for a thirteen-year-old with a spray can, equity isn't full price or a pass. It's a share he can actually carry.

how: The Qur'an (49:9) tells believers to make peace between quarreling parties with justice and to act equitably; Muslims bring that to family disputes and community mediation.

o: the Judge who punishes every wrong
the Equitable, who gives each their due
the Generous, who gives all the same

games.q: a level scale, two neighbors — tap the pairs.
p: no favor for poor or mighty

s: the Qur'an says hatred of a people must not push you into injustice
"let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly."
Leviticus 19:15 tells judges to lean toward the poor
it says not to respect the person of the poor, nor honor the mighty: no lean either way.
the Qur'an and Leviticus say the same thing word for word
they share a level scale; Leviticus names status as the pull, the Qur'an names hatred.

games.q: your little sister broke your lamp. your parents ask you what's fair. you are furious. what does 5:8 point you toward?
o: the full cost; anger is fair when you're the one who was wronged.
a share she can actually carry, chosen as if you weren't angry.
nothing at all, since she's younger and didn't mean it.
games.why: 5:8 names anger, hatred, as the thing that tips the scale. the equitable answer isn't full price or a pass; it's her real due.

practice: Pick one person you're finding it hard to be fair to this week. Name, in one honest sentence, what fair would look like, and then name what tilts you: anger, liking them, old history.
Decide one thing you'll do when you feel the tilt, and hold that plan quietly through the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Muqsit. The Equitable: each given their due, with no hand pressing on the scale, not even our own.

orig.note: Arabic: the Equitable, from the traditional list of the Names; 49:9 says Allah loves al-muqsitin, the equitable.

carryVoice: Hold onto it: equitable, even when your own hand is shaking near the scale. That's fifteen sixty.
